query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a modest amount of molybdenum to a base equiatomic CrCoNiFe high‐entropy alloy will improve its overall performance for aerospace fastener applications by enhancing mechanical durability, reducing room‐temperature creep, and increasing corrosion resistance through the promotion of sluggish diffusion and solution strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline CrCoNiFe high‐entropy alloy produced without Mo addition that shows moderate yield strength, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a modest addition of Mo during alloy synthesis so that Mo replaces a corresponding fraction of one or more of the base elements.
generation.conditions: Material tested at room temperature under static and cyclic mechanical loading and in a saline environment simulating corrosive aerospace conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Mo atoms are expected to promote local chemical ordering and enhance solution strengthening; they may also induce the formation of fine, uniformly dispersed Mo-rich features that hinder dislocation motion and reduce atomic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: The Mo addition retards atomic diffusion (introducing sluggish diffusion), enhances yield strength via solid solution and precipitation effects, and promotes formation of a more stable, protective passive oxide film that improves corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the Mo-modified alloy is anticipated to exhibit roughly a 20% improvement in yield strength, a measurable reduction in room-temperature creep deformation, and lower corrosion current densities in NaCl due to a more robust passive film.
generation.baseline: The performance of the original CrCoNiFe alloy with 0% Mo under identical processing and testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The expected improvements apply under controlled processing and standard laboratory test conditions; deviations may occur due to variations in processing parameters or testing environments typical for aerospace fasteners.
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvement percentages in mechanical and corrosion properties are uncertain and may vary with processing conditions and precise Mo content; further optimization of the Mo level might be necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of otherwise identical high-entropy alloy samples: one with the baseline CrCoNiFe composition and one with 5 at% Mo substituted into the alloy. Process both sets under identical conditions. Then, perform room-temperature tensile tests (for yield strength and ductility), nano-indentation creep tests at a fixed load (to assess creep displacement over time), and potentiodynamic polarization tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (to gauge corrosion potential and current density).
measurements: Yield strength and ductility from tensile tests
Creep displacement versus time from nano-indentation tests
Corrosion potential and corrosion current density from polarization tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-added alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., >10% increase in yield strength, a clear reduction in creep displacement, and improved corrosion parameters such as a higher corrosion potential/lower current density) compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent a new class of alloys that consist of more than four alloying elements in close to equiatomic concentrations (). The diverse compositional possibilities of HEAs, combined with appropriate heat treatment conditions, offer the potential to develop new alloys with a combination of remarkable properties such as outstanding mechanical properties, high-hydrogen absorption capacity, and robust resistance to corrosion and radiation (). The refractory HEAs (RHEAs) based on refractory elements were proposed by Senkov et al. () as a new class of high-temperature structural alloys that might surpass the capabilities of nickel-based superalloys. RHEAs are emerging as prominent contenders in diverse industries, notably in the nuclear and aerospace sectors (, ).

AbstractHighly entropy alloys (HEAs) are novel materials that have great potential for application in aerospace and marine engineering due to their superior mechanical properties and benefits over conventional materials. NiCrCoFe, also referred to as Ni-based HEA, has exceptional low-temperature strength and microstructural stability. However, HEAs have limited corrosion resistance in some environments, such as a 3.5 wt% sodium chloride (NaCl) solution. Adding corrosion-resistant elements such as molybdenum (Mo) to HEAs is expected to increase their corrosion resistance in a variety of corrosive environments. Metal additive manufacturing reduces production times compared to casting and eliminates shrinkage issues, making it ideal for producing homogeneous HEA. This study used directed energy deposition (DED) to create Cr25-xCo25Ni25Fe25Mox (x = 0, 5, 10%) HEAs. Tensile strength and potentiodynamic polarization tests were used to assess the materials’ mechanical properties and corrosion resistance.
